opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. I think about it this way: the fields most worth changing with AI are the ones that already have very deep, very rigorous foundations, places where humans have built centuries of knowledge but where progress is bottlenecked by how much careful reasoning a person can do in a lifetime.

Our approach isn't to come in and say, "AI will replace the experts." That framing misunderstands how established fields work. Mathematics, for example, has its own standards of truth, its own culture of proof, its own taste for what counts as an interesting problem. If you ignore that, you build something flashy that the community doesn't trust and won't use. So we start from deep respect for the field's internal logic, and we ask what AI can do *within* that logic that wasn't possible before.

For us, a few principles follow from that.

First, **verifiability**. In an established field, trust is everything. In math we're lucky, because a proof can be checked, and with formal languages it can be checked by a machine. So rather than building a system that just sounds right, we want one whose outputs can be verified. That turns AI from an oracle you have to believe into a collaborator whose work you can audit.

Second, **taking the hardest version of the problem seriously**. It's tempting to pick the easy, commercial slice of a field. But I believe the way to really change a field is to aim at its core challenge. If you can build systems that reason reliably at the frontier, the applications downstream, in software verification, science, engineering, come naturally.

Third, **building with the community, not around it**. The people who've spent decades in a field know where the real pain points are. Some of the most valuable things AI can do are unglamorous: formalizing existing knowledge, checking long arguments, searching through huge spaces of possibilities so a human can focus on the creative leap.

And finally, a bit of patience. Established fields didn't become established overnight, and they won't be transformed overnight. I'd rather build something foundational that compounds over ten or twenty years than something that makes headlines for a month. If we do it right, the goal is that a mathematician, or a scientist, ten years from now has a reasoning partner that makes them dramatically more ambitious about the questions they're willing to ask. That, to me, is what changing a field really means.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I think about how we approached founding Axiom, the starting point wasn't really "let's apply AI to mathematics." It was almost the reverse. I spent years inside pure mathematics, and the thing that struck me was how much of the discipline's actual daily work is invisible from the outside. People imagine a mathematician sitting alone having flashes of insight. In reality, an enormous share of the work is careful, structured, almost mechanical: checking that a lemma really holds, searching for a counterexample, verifying that a step you believe is obvious actually survives scrutiny. That part of the process is slow, it is error-prone, and it is exactly the kind of thing where a machine could be a genuine collaborator rather than a toy.

So the founding thesis was that mathematics is a uniquely good place for AI to change a field, because it has something almost no other domain has: a notion of correctness that can be formally verified. In most fields, when a model produces an answer, you have to trust it or go check it by hand. In math, if you work inside a formal proof system like Lean, a proof either compiles or it doesn't. There is no ambiguity. That gives you a training signal and a trust mechanism at the same time. It means the model can be wrong a thousand times in private and only show you the one thing that is actually correct. For a field built on rigor, that property is everything.

The second thing I understood early is that you cannot change an established field from the outside. Mathematicians are, rightly, skeptical. They have spent their lives developing taste about what is interesting and what is true, and a tool that generates plausible-sounding nonsense is worse than useless to them. So our approach was never to replace that judgment. It was to build something that respects the culture of the field, that speaks its language, both literally in the formal sense and culturally in terms of what counts as a meaningful contribution. We wanted mathematicians to look at the output and recognize it as real mathematics, not as a statistical imitation of it.

And the third piece, which I think is the one people underestimate, is that changing a field means changing who gets to participate in it. Right now, deep mathematical research is gated by access: to the right advisors, the right institutions, the accumulated oral tradition that never makes it into textbooks. If a system can hold that knowledge and reason with it reliably, a student somewhere without those connections can push on a real problem. To me that is as much a part of the mission as any benchmark result.

So when I say we are using AI to change mathematics, what I really mean is this: we are taking the one intellectual field where truth is checkable, building systems that can be trusted precisely because they can be verified, and doing it in a way that works with the field's own standards rather than against them. If we get that right in mathematics, I think it becomes the template for how you do it anywhere else that rigor matters.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is to ask what a field is fundamentally trying to accomplish, and then examine which parts of the way it works reflect real constraints and which are habits built around older tools. With AI, some of those constraints may change, so there’s an opportunity to rethink the process rather than simply make an existing step faster.

But that requires working closely with people who understand the field. You need to know where judgment matters, what mistakes cost, and what would actually make the technology useful. To me, the founding approach is to pair that willingness to rethink things with a very concrete problem—and let results tell you whether you’re creating meaningful change.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, the starting point is the problem, rather than the technology. In an established field, there’s usually a reason people work the way they do. So before asking what AI can automate, we need to understand where people get stuck, what requires judgment, and what a better outcome would actually look like.

Then we can ask whether AI makes a fundamentally different approach possible. I think that takes both technical ambition and humility: ambition about what we could build, and humility about how much we need to learn from the people doing the work. The goal is to create something they find useful and can trust.
